subject: Domain redundancy liability & RTO/RPO scope — proposal
content:

Cc: Procurement Team <procurement@fintrust.com>

Subject: Domain redundancy liability & RTO/RPO scope — proposal

Hi Maria / FinTrust procurement team,

Thanks again for the conversation yesterday. Per our follow-up, attached is a proposed addendum that narrows multi-region failover commitments to exclude certain customer-specific failure domains where data residency or regional regulatory controls prevent pre-warmed standby capacity. Key highlights upfront so you don’t need to open the PDF right away: 

- Proposed regional RTO for automatic failover: 60 minutes (warm-standby eligible regions).
- Proposed RPO: 15 minutes for warm-standby regions; 24 hours for cold-standby recovery where on-demand provisioning is required.
- Activation eligibility: Warm standby only in regions where the customer has provided cross-border transfer consent and KMS access; otherwise recovery will be cold-standby with the longer RTO/RPO above.
- Liability carveout: For any failover that is prevented by third-party regulatory restrictions or customer-controlled network boundary (e.g., air-gapped vaults), we propose limiting SLA credits to service usage refunds only (no uptime-related penalties).

I’ve attached a short capacity matrix with estimates of pre-warmed GPU pools and expected activation times by region. Please review and tell us which failure domains you consider non-negotiable for FinTrust (data sovereignty zones, encrypted vaults under local KMS, etc.). If this direction looks acceptable, we can route the addendum to your procurement/contact for signature.

Thanks,
Naomi Feldman
Head of Strategic Accounts — Redwood Inference

Hi Naomi,

Thanks for the quick follow-up and the attachments. A few clarification requests before we loop legal/procurement: 

1) Can you expand on what you mean by "failure domain" in the addendum? Is this a physical AZ boundary, an entire country region, or something else?
2) The 60-minute RTO for warm-standby — is that achievable under both typical and peak traffic scenarios? Do you have historical activation metrics for similar customers?
3) For cold-standby where you list 24 hours, is there a path to reduce that to 8–12 hours with additional reserved capacity (we can evaluate the cost tradeoff).

Happy to have a quick call today if that helps.

Best,
Maria
Head of Infrastructure — FinTrust

Subject: Re: Domain redundancy liability & RTO/RPO scope — proposal

Maria — thanks for the questions. Quick answers and context below; Karthik has added a capacity/activation breakdown in his reply.

1) Failure domain definition: For this addendum we propose defining "failure domain" as the region-level grouping used for routing and data residency (e.g., EU-WEST as a region) plus any customer-owned network boundary that prevents pre-provisioning (air-gapped vaults, on-prem KMS). In practice that means the region (country-level) is the primary determinant; AZ-level incidents inside the same region are covered by our standard intra-region redundancy.

2) 60-minute RTO feasibility: Yes for warm-standby when pre-warmed capacity is held and cross-region routing is permitted. Activation includes DNS propagation, pre-warmed cache warm-up, and KV-cache population; we optimize for <60m on customer traffic shapes similar to yours. We include a 20% buffer for surge.

3) Cold-standby timelines: Reducing to 8–12 hours requires reserved capacity and a prioritized provisioning lane. We can model this for you with associated incremental monthly fees (shown in the capacity matrix).

Next step: Karthik — can you add the region-by-region activation times and the expected incremental cost to move from 24h cold to 12h cold?

Naomi

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Domain redundancy liability & RTO/RPO scope — proposal

Thanks Naomi — adding the technical detail here. I pulled numbers from our last three warm-standby activations with regulated customers. Notes below are operational median values; we can provide the raw activation traces if you want.

- EU-WEST (warm-standby pre-warmed, cross-region routing allowed): median activation time = 32 minutes; 95th percentile = 58 minutes. Primary steps: routing switch (5–12m), behind-the-scenes model KV restore (8–20m depending on sequence length), cache warm-up (10–20m), health checks and traffic ramp (5–10m).
- EU-NORTH (sparser capacity): median = 45m; 95th = 72m. If we reserve additional pre-warmed nodes (+30% capacity) we estimate median falls to 28m and 95th to 50m.
- Cold-standby reprovisioning (when regulatory boundary prevents pre-warm): typical reprovision + data sync pipeline = 18–36 hours; with prioritized provisioning lane + incremental reserved capacity we can target 10–12 hours.

Operational controls we recommend adding to the addendum so SLA expectations are aligned: 
- Customer must maintain a documented list of failure domains where cross-border transfer consent is withheld.
- Customer to provide KMS access or bring-your-own-key (BYOK) documentation for any warmed region.
- Redwood will maintain a weekly activation readiness test for all warm-standby regions (non-prod traffic) with results shared in the Console. Failures to maintain readiness due to customer-controlled configuration will invalidate warm-standby RTO guarantees.

Liability carveout rationale: When a customer refuses cross-border transfer or cannot permit KMS access, we cannot pre-warm nodes in the protected domain without violating constraints. In those cases the service model switches to cold-standby and the SLA should reflect the longer recovery. We propose the liability limit be defined as service fee credits only.

Attachments: warm-standby-capacity-matrix.csv (shows cost deltas by region for +20% and +30% pre-warm options).

Happy to join a quick call to walk through the activation traces.

— Karthik
Principal Engineer — Serving Runtime

Maria / procurement team —

Appreciate the thoughtful questions. Summary and next steps: 

- We will mark EU-WEST and EU-NORTH as warm-standby eligible provided FinTrust confirms KMS/BYOK access and cross-border transfer consent for the regions in scope.
- If FinTrust requires the protected failure domain (you mentioned a specific vault) to remain air-gapped, that domain will be classified as cold-standby with an RTO target of 10–12 hours if you take the prioritized provisioning option, otherwise default to 24 hours.
- Proposed change to liability: for cold-standby activations caused by customer-controlled restrictions, SLA remedies limited to fees credits. For warm-standby activations that miss the SLA due to Redwood operational issues, full SLA credit schedule in the addendum applies.

Action items: 
1) Maria — please confirm the list of protected failure domains and whether procurement wants us to price the prioritized provisioning lane (we included cost rows in the CSV).
2) Procurement — if acceptable, we can open the DocuSign envelope and route for signature (link below). Once signed we will schedule the readiness tests and update the Console to show the warm-standby readiness status.
